questions.question: You receive an email that says your account will be closed within 30 minutes unless you “verify now.” What should you do first?

choices.label: Click the link quickly so you don't lose access
Slow down and verify independently using a trusted channel
Reply to the sender and ask for more time
Enter your password to confirm it’s you

questions.explanation: Urgency is a common manipulation tactic. Verify through trusted channels before interacting.

questions.question: A message threatens disciplinary action and says you’ve already violated policy. Which response best protects you?

choices.label: Follow the instructions immediately to avoid consequences
Take a breath and verify the claim through official channels
Forward the message to coworkers to confirm details
Complete any login or form request from the message
choices.hint: Credentials should never be entered from untrusted links.

questions.explanation: Intimidation aims to stop you from questioning. Verify independently.

questions.question: Your manager emails you to wire money “right away” and says to bypass normal approval steps. What is the safest action?

choices.label: Trust the email because it appears to be from leadership
Verify the request via a separate trusted channel, then follow process
Reply to the manager using the same email thread
Click the embedded link to “confirm instructions”

questions.explanation: Even authority-based requests must be verified independently and routed through standard process.

questions.question: A text says you won a limited-time reward and asks you to click a link to claim it. What's the best next step?

choices.label: Click immediately to avoid missing out
Verify the offer using official channels before interacting
Share the link with friends so they can confirm
Reply with your account details so it can be claimed

questions.explanation: Scarcity is a tactic. Verify safely before clicking or entering details.

questions.question: Which scenario most closely matches credential phishing?

choices.label: A fake login page asks you to enter your username and password
A meeting invite lists agenda items with no links
An internal document is shared through an approved system
A password manager warns you your password was changed

questions.explanation: Credential phishing aims to capture login credentials through fake pages or forms.

questions.question: A message requests a one-time code (OTP) sent via SMS to “verify your identity.” Why is this dangerous?

choices.label: OTP codes never matter for account security
Attackers can use OTP codes to take over accounts
choices.hint: This is a common takeover method.

choices.label: OTP codes are only used for marketing verification
OTP codes are shared with IT automatically

questions.explanation: OTP codes can be used to bypass authentication and complete account compromise.

questions.question: Which is the best sign you should treat a message as suspicious?

choices.label: It provides clear, verifiable details and allows time to check
It tells you not to contact support and to act immediately
choices.hint: Bypassing verification is a red flag.

choices.label: It uses your correct name and includes no links
It’s written politely and with good grammar

questions.explanation: Phishers often try to prevent you from verifying.

questions.question: What should you NEVER do because of intimidation or threats?

choices.label: Enter credentials from a link or form in the message
choices.hint: Credentials should be entered only through trusted flows.

choices.label: Verify independently using official channels
Report it through approved mechanisms
Take time to assess before acting

questions.explanation: Threats should not change your security behavior—never submit credentials via suspicious links.

questions.question: If you’re asked to pay a new vendor and the instructions arrived via email, what’s the safest approach?

choices.label: Update payment details based only on the email
choices.hint: High risk if attacker is impersonating.

choices.label: Verify the vendor/payment change through your organization’s normal procurement/finance process
Reply with bank details so they can confirm
Assume the sender is genuine if the signature looks right

questions.explanation: Payment changes must go through standard verification to prevent fraud.

questions.question: What best describes spear phishing?

choices.label: Mass emails with random details sent to everyone
Messages tailored to a specific person or department to appear credible
Only phone calls with no email involvement
choices.hint: Spear phishing is not limited to one channel.

choices.label: Always obvious scams with misspellings

questions.explanation: Spear phishing is targeted and designed to increase trust.
